reasons.C1: Tests whether human-derived antitrust levers transfer to LLM sellers; policy-relevant, though LLM replication of economics experiments is an established genre.
reasons.C2: Positive control, placebo arm, human and scripted baselines, bootstrap intervals, second model; weakened by one seed per regime and few reward cartels.
reasons.C3: Scorecard framing and human-beside-model figure make results legible; placebo versus laissez-faire numbers need clearer reconciliation.

levers.C1: Show the framing effect generalises across providers and derive a concrete recommendation authorities could adopt for algorithmic sellers.
levers.C2: Run multiple seeds per regime, add a second provider, and enlarge reward and leniency cartel counts for tighter intervals.
levers.C3: Explain the placebo result upfront as the headline mechanism and state each comparison's sample in one table.

X9.verdict: Most complete entry: real controlled experiment with positive control and placebo; the framing finding is genuinely interesting for evaluators.

reasons.C1: Planted price-fixing offer with say-versus-do measurement is a sensible eval design, but similar elicitation setups exist.
reasons.C2: No core run, empty run-log folder, invented demo data; hundreds of tests do not substitute for results.
reasons.C3: Report is a placeholder skeleton; cannot determine findings because none exist yet.

levers.C1: Show a surprising say-do gap across several models that changes how deployers should monitor pricing agents.
levers.C2: Execute the preregistered 60 games, pass the positive-control gate, and report Wilson intervals per condition.
levers.C3: Write the report with problem, method, results per condition, and limitations, using real run data only.

J2.verdict: Good preregistered design, but nothing has actually been run; I cannot score results that do not exist.

reasons.C1: Countermeasures for latent-vector steganography matter for oversight, but snapping to embeddings defeating a non-adaptive channel is expected.
reasons.C2: Held-out data, reproduce log matching checkpoints, null and shuffled-label controls; but no collusion game and channels pre-trained before sprint.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 delivers the core claim instantly; limitations stated clearly; scope versus sprint contribution needs sharper separation.

levers.C1: Train channels adaptively against snapping and show whether a robust countermeasure survives, inside an actual collusion task.
levers.C2: Embed the channel in a collusion game with a collusion positive control and add significance tests across more seeds.
levers.C3: Separate pre-sprint work from sprint contributions in one explicit table at the start of the report.

W2.verdict: Rigorous, clean evaluation work, but on a carrier not colluding agents, and the main result is unsurprising for non-adaptive channels.

reasons.C1: Real-world detection on payment ledgers is useful for operators, but wallets are not shown to be AI agents colluding.
reasons.C2: Held-out split, permutation test, synthetic rings; but ten test families, wide intervals, label leakage, label-independent rule insignificant.
reasons.C3: Core claims and limitations clear; 17-page report and absent demo make the main signal harder to extract.

levers.C1: Establish that flagged wallets are LLM agents and show the detector catches agent-driven self-funding rings specifically.
levers.C2: Obtain independent labels from another team and evaluate on more families with features disjoint from labelling evidence.
levers.C3: Lead with one figure of held-out performance against baselines and trim the body to essential results.

M4.verdict: Practical detector with honest stats, but leaky labels and no proof these are AI agents keep it off-topic and fragile.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions settling or fighting is a neglected question beyond single-coalition-versus-principal setups; could open a direction.
reasons.C2: 144 episodes, no-rival arm, seeds and intervals; but no positive control, post-freeze measure change, borderline p = 0.055.
reasons.C3: Report not seen; only README and tables, so the story and conclusions are hard to reconstruct.

levers.C1: Show coalitions emerge uninstructed and that rivalry measurably changes cohesion, across more than one grid model.
levers.C2: Add a positive control for bloc formation, preregister the corrected defection measure, and power the key comparison.
levers.C3: Deliver the report with a clear headline finding, outcome-class figure, and the required limitations and dual-use appendix.

W5.verdict: Interesting new question with a decent grid, but missing positive control and report leave the claims unsupported for now.
